props.title: All Through the Night
props.initialSlug: Bogart hunts Nazi spies in NYC nightclub underworld

sections.content: All Through the Night stands as a fascinating hybrid of gangster film and wartime propaganda, featuring Humphrey Bogart as a New York gambler who stumbles upon a Nazi spy ring. Released just weeks after Pearl Harbor, it bridges Warner Bros.' signature gangster pictures like The Maltese Falcon (1941) with the studio's shift toward anti-Nazi messaging. The film cleverly repurposes mobster movie tropes - with street-smart criminals becoming unlikely patriots, fighting an even worse evil than themselves.

sections.content: Director Vincent Sherman deftly balances suspense with dark comedy, allowing Bogart's "Gloves" Donahue to crack wise even as he uncovers deadly serious Nazi plots. The supporting cast includes several actors who fled Nazi Germany, including Conrad Veidt and Peter Lorre, adding gravitas to the film's anti-fascist themes. Their real-life experiences inform the authentic menace they bring to their roles.

The film represents a crucial transition point in 1940s Hollywood, as the industry shifted from isolation to active wartime messaging. Like Casablanca (1942) and Watch on the Rhine (1943), it shows American cinema processing the Nazi threat through genre conventions - in this case, merging the gangster film's urban grit with spy thriller elements. SUBHEAD: The Wartime Transformation of the Gangster Film

sections.content: All Through the Night exemplifies how Hollywood crime films evolved during WWII. Where earlier gangster pictures like The Public Enemy (1931) portrayed criminals as social menaces, wartime entries often recast underworld figures as rough-edged patriots. This film's gang of gamblers and racketeers become unlikely heroes defending America, presaging later WWII films like OSS (1946) and O.S.S. (1946) that glorified covert operations.
